title: Anonymity is user-facing only; the backend keeps identity and messages
context: An anonymous campus chat needs moderation, and moderation needs to know who sent what.
options: Anonymous to other users only
Anonymous to the operator as well
decision: Other users see only a pseudonym. The backend retains the identity mapping and message data for moderation.
rationale: The audience is one college, a known and bounded user base. The privacy bar is that other users cannot identify you, not that the operator cannot.
tradeoffs: Users must trust the operator with their identity. A retention policy and clear wording at sign-in are required.

title: Phase 1 is a single-campus anonymous chat; the dating and reveal mechanic is deferred
context: The earlier prototype reached about 400 users in its first day or two, then usage dropped off. The long-term idea is a chat-first dating app.
options: Build chat and dating together
Chat first, dating later
decision: Build anonymous 1:1 and group chat for one campus first. Revisit the reveal mechanic only with real usage data.
rationale: Retention has to be proven on the simpler product before adding a riskier one.
tradeoffs: Phase 1 has to be valuable on its own, not just a funnel to a later feature.

title: Independent services from the start, all written in Go
context: The project is both a real product and a deliberate exercise in distributed systems.
options: Monolith, split later
Independent services from day one
decision: Seven services: gateway, identity, matching, chat, presence, moderation, persistence-worker. Go everywhere.
rationale: Service boundaries, contracts between services and independent deployment are the things being learned; a monolith would not exercise them.
tradeoffs: More moving parts and more operational work than a monolith for a solo developer at this scale.

title: gRPC between services, with protobuf contracts managed by buf
context: Services need typed contracts that both sides agree on.
options: gRPC with protobuf
REST with JSON
decision: All internal calls are gRPC. The .proto files under proto/ are the source of truth; buf generates Go stubs into proto/gen/go.
rationale: Typed contracts, generated clients and servers, and streaming support. buf replaces hand-written protoc invocations.
tradeoffs: Browsers cannot call gRPC directly, so the gateway has to translate HTTP and WebSocket traffic. Proto changes affect every service.

title: RabbitMQ as the message broker
context: Live delivery must not wait on the database write, so delivery and persistence need to be decoupled.
options: RabbitMQ
Kafka
NATS
decision: RabbitMQ carries chat messages and moderation events to the persistence worker.
rationale: Simpler to operate alone than Kafka at this scale.
tradeoffs: Queue semantics rather than a replayable log.

title: Postgres is the source of truth, accessed through repository interfaces
context: The PRD asks for a persistence layer that can be swapped later.
options: Raw SQL in business logic
Repository interface per store
decision: Each service reaches its store through an interface (for example AccountStore) with a Postgres implementation behind it.
rationale: Swapping the store changes one implementation, not the service. It also allows in-memory fakes in unit tests.
tradeoffs: One extra layer per store. Fakes cannot reproduce real database behaviour (see INC-0003).

title: Redis for presence, live fan-out, caches and the match queue
context: Several features need fast, short-lived shared state across service instances.
options: Redis
In-process memory only
decision: Redis holds presence counters, pub/sub channels for live delivery, the invite-code cache and the match queue.
rationale: Shared in-memory state that every instance can reach; none of it is the source of truth.
tradeoffs: Redis data can be lost on restart and must be rebuildable.

title: Deploy on k3s running on VPS nodes
context: The pilot needs real Kubernetes at low cost.
options: k3s on VPS
Managed Kubernetes (EKS or GKE)
decision: A small k3s cluster on one or two VPS nodes, with managed Postgres.
rationale: Standard Kubernetes at a fraction of the cost of a managed control plane.
tradeoffs: The cluster has to be operated by hand.

title: Monorepo with a Go workspace and one module per service
context: Services must build and deploy independently but share generated proto code and small packages during development.
options: One Go module for the whole repo
One module per service tied together by go.work
Separate repositories
decision: go.work lists pkg, proto/gen/go and each service as its own module.
rationale: Each service keeps its own dependencies and build, and local imports resolve from disk without publishing or replace directives.
tradeoffs: In workspace mode Go resolves a single version of each dependency across all modules, so one module can raise the version for the others (see INC-0004).

title: Pin dependencies to versions the installed Go toolchain can build, and set GOTOOLCHAIN=local in CI
context: See INC-0001: a dependency requiring a newer Go version triggered a toolchain download that kept failing.
options: Always use @latest
Pin to versions compatible with the installed toolchain
decision: grpc was pinned to v1.71.1 and pgx to v5.8.0. CI sets GOTOOLCHAIN=local so a version mismatch fails fast.
rationale: A clear error is better than a silent, flaky toolchain download.
tradeoffs: Pinned versions drift behind upstream and need periodic review.

title: Badge verification checks a signed OIDC ID token, not a typed email address
context: The badge gates gender-filtered matching, so it has to prove ownership of a college account.
options: User types their college email
Emailed code or magic link
Signed ID token from the identity provider
decision: VerifyBadge takes an ID token and verifies it with a generic OIDC library (go-oidc), configured with the issuer URL.
rationale: A typed email proves nothing. A signed token can be verified without handling passwords, and a generic library keeps the provider swappable.
tradeoffs: Depends on the college's identity provider allowing third-party sign-in (confirmed for KIIT in DEC-0027).

title: Schema migrations are embedded in the binary and run at startup
context: Schema changes need an ordered, recorded history that travels with the service.
options: Run SQL by hand
Separate migration job
Embedded migrations run on startup
decision: golang-migrate applies the .sql files embedded with go:embed when the service starts.
rationale: The container image carries its own schema history. golang-migrate takes a Postgres advisory lock, so several replicas starting together stay safe.
tradeoffs: Startup depends on the database being reachable, and a bad migration blocks startup.

title: A shared gRPC logging interceptor is the foundation for metrics and tracing
context: Every service needs one structured log line per request, and later a trace span and a duration metric at the same point.
options: Log inside each handler
One shared interceptor
decision: pkg/grpclog provides a unary server interceptor that logs method, status code and duration as JSON through log/slog.
rationale: The interceptor is the single place every request passes through, so tracing and metrics extend it instead of adding a second mechanism.
tradeoffs: It covers unary calls only; streaming calls need their own interceptor.

title: go get grpc@latest required a Go toolchain download that kept failing
what_happened: go get google.golang.org/grpc@latest pulled v1.83.1, which requires Go 1.25. The installed toolchain was 1.24.3, so Go tried to download go1.25.0 and the download failed repeatedly on the network. pgx's latest release had the same requirement.
impact: Builds were blocked until the dependency versions were pinned.
root_cause: Since Go 1.21 the go directive in a dependency's go.mod is a real minimum, and GOTOOLCHAIN=auto silently downloads a newer toolchain. Leftover indirect requirement lines also kept transitive versions high after the pin.
resolution: Pinned grpc to v1.71.1 and pgx to v5.8.0, lowered the leftover indirect requirements explicitly, and set GOTOOLCHAIN=local in CI.
lessons: Do not run @latest by reflex. GOTOOLCHAIN=local turns a confusing network timeout into a clear version error.

title: go build ./... from the repo root does not span workspace modules
what_happened: Running go build ./services/... from the repo root failed with 'directory prefix services does not contain modules listed in go.work'.
impact: A single root-level build or test command could not be used locally or in CI.
root_cause: The ./... pattern does not expand across a directory that is not itself a module root.
resolution: Build and test each module from its own directory. CI runs one matrix job per module.
lessons: Per-module builds match how each service is built for deployment anyway.

title: GetAccount returned Internal and leaked a database error for a malformed account ID
what_happened: Calling GetAccount with a non-UUID ID against real Postgres returned codes.Internal with the raw Postgres error text instead of NotFound.
impact: Internal database details were exposed to callers, and a client error was reported as a server error.
root_cause: Postgres rejects a malformed UUID literal (error 22P02) before the query runs. The in-memory fake store used by the unit tests could not reproduce that path.
resolution: isNotFound in the Postgres store now maps error 22P02 to ErrNotFound.
lessons: Unit tests against fakes do not cover real database behaviour. The bug was found only by running the service against real Postgres with grpcurl; integration tests are still missing.

title: The gateway is the only public entry point and uses two separate tokens
context: Browsers cannot speak gRPC, and internal services should not be reachable from outside.
options: Every service validates client tokens
Only the gateway faces clients
decision: The gateway translates HTTP and WebSocket traffic to gRPC and is the whole trust boundary. Google's ID token is used once, for verification; the gateway's own session token is used for everything afterwards.
rationale: One place to enforce authentication and rate limits. Internal services trust the account ID the gateway passes.
tradeoffs: A flaw in the gateway exposes everything behind it.

title: Live delivery across gateway instances goes through Redis pub/sub
context: Two people in one chat can be connected to different gateway instances, and neither instance can reach the other's sockets.
options: Pin each room to one gateway instance
Redis pub/sub fan-out with a local connection registry per instance
decision: The chat service publishes to a Redis channel per room. Each gateway instance subscribes only to rooms it has local clients in.
rationale: The chat service does not need to know which instance holds a connection, and gateways can scale horizontally.
tradeoffs: Redis pub/sub does not store messages; a disconnected client misses them unless history is loaded separately.

title: Significant plan changes are discussed and agreed before anything is built
context: The project is a learning vehicle as well as a product, and the maintainer wants to take part in each decision.
options: Build first and review afterwards
Discuss, decide, then build
decision: Design questions are settled in discussion, one at a time, with a recommendation for each. Agreed decisions are logged here before implementation starts.
rationale: Decisions made together are understood and can be defended later.
tradeoffs: Planning takes longer before the first line of code.

title: External facts are verified against official documentation before they are stated
context: See INC-0005. Budget and architecture calculations depend on pricing, limits and product behaviour being correct.
options: State from memory with caveats
Verify first and cite the source
decision: No claim about an outside product or service is made without checking its current official documentation. Anything that cannot be verified is labelled unverified.
rationale: One wrong number can invalidate a budget or a design.
tradeoffs: Planning is slower, and some answers stay unverified until a source is found.

title: Keep a small, professional set of docs and remove the knowledge base
context: docs/ had grown to a 13-article knowledge base plus several design documents that nobody would read.
options: Keep growing the knowledge base
A few maintained documents plus a decision log
decision: Root: README, CONTRIBUTING, AGENTS.md, SECURITY, CODE_OF_CONDUCT, LICENSE. docs/: PRD, ARCHITECTURE, PLAN and this log. docs/kb and docs/CONCEPT.md are removed; git history keeps them. CLAUDE.md only imports AGENTS.md.
rationale: Short documents get read and stay accurate. One rules file serves every AI tool and every human contributor.
tradeoffs: Tutorial-style explanations no longer live in the repo; reasoning is captured here in shorter form.

title: Decisions and incidents are recorded in one JSONL log
context: Decisions and their reasons were scattered across prose and chat history.
options: Prose documents
One Markdown ADR file per decision
A single JSONL log
decision: docs/decisions.jsonl holds one JSON object per line: decisions in the style of architecture decision records, incidents as short postmortems. Interview preparation is generated from this file instead of kept separately.
rationale: Append-only, easy to query, and readable by tools. A single source avoids two files drifting apart.
tradeoffs: Long lines are awkward to read without a tool such as jq.

title: Kafka replaces RabbitMQ; Redis pub/sub stays for live delivery
context: The maintainer is learning Kafka and wants to use it here. No code depended on RabbitMQ yet, so the switch only touched docs and the local compose file.
options: Kafka
RabbitMQ queues
RabbitMQ Streams
NATS
decision: Kafka carries durable events (chat messages, moderation events) to independent consumers. Redis pub/sub remains the low-latency path to connected clients.
rationale: Learning Kafka is an explicit goal, and Kafka is built around a retained log that several consumers read independently with per-key ordering. RabbitMQ Streams offer similar semantics, so this is not a claim that RabbitMQ could not do the job.
tradeoffs: More memory and operational work than RabbitMQ. On the pilot budget it runs as a single broker, so there is no replication.

title: The project is open source from day one
context: The repository is public and other people or AI tools may contribute.
options: Private until launch
Public from the start
decision: Develop in the open, with contribution, security and conduct documents in place from the first PR. The license is still to be chosen.
rationale: Public code builds trust in an anonymous app, because the claim about what is stored can be checked. It is also a portfolio piece.
tradeoffs: Anyone can read how the protections work, so secrets must never be committed and the pre-launch security review matters more.

title: GitHub Flow with CI as the merge gate
context: Earlier commits went straight to main.
options: Commit to main
Branch, pull request, CI, merge
decision: Every change goes through a short-lived branch and a pull request. CI must pass before merge. Pull requests are squash-merged with a Conventional Commits title. Approvals are not required while there is one maintainer.
rationale: Tested, reviewable history. GitHub does not let authors approve their own pull requests, so requiring approvals would lock out a solo maintainer.
tradeoffs: Slightly more ceremony for small changes.

title: Run the pilot on Google Cloud trial credits, on Kubernetes, and build it to be portable
context: A Google Cloud free trial provides $300 of credit over 90 days, ending 2026-12-25. Unused credit expires, and resources are stopped when the trial ends.
options: k3s on VPS from the start
Google Cloud for the pilot, then migrate
decision: Deploy the pilot to Kubernetes on Google Cloud. Move off between 2026-12-15 and 2026-12-18. Everything runs inside Kubernetes and is defined as code, and no Google-only managed services are used.
rationale: Real infrastructure at no cost for the pilot. Portability turns the December move into recreate, restore and repoint.
tradeoffs: A hard deadline, and a migration to plan. Cluster layout and cost are still to be designed.

title: v1 is the usable product plus monitoring, launched by 2026-10-15
context: The earlier prototype's best data came from its launch spike, and monitoring data cannot be collected after the fact.
options: Ship first and add monitoring later
Monitoring live before launch
decision: Monitoring is part of v1 and is running before the first real user. Closed beta on 2026-10-13 and 14, public launch by 2026-10-15. If something has to slip, the date slips, not safety features or monitoring.
rationale: Launch-day numbers are the most valuable and are lost if nothing is recording.
tradeoffs: More work before launch on a short timeline.

title: No performance or usage number is claimed without saved evidence
context: The project doubles as a portfolio piece, and trial infrastructure disappears when the trial ends.
options: Estimate numbers
Record measured numbers with their method
decision: A number is only quoted if a dated artefact with its method is committed to the repo: a load-test result, a dashboard export or a query result.
rationale: Claims stay checkable after the infrastructure is gone.
tradeoffs: Evidence has to be exported during the pilot, not afterwards.

title: Two tiers: guests and KIIT-verified users, with guest accounts upgraded in place
context: The question was whether to restrict the app to college accounts. Options weighed were KIIT sign-in for everyone, any Google account, fully open, or two tiers.
options: Two tiers
KIIT sign-in for everyone
Any Google account required
Fully open
decision: Anyone can join as a guest with a pseudonym and use group rooms and random 1:1 matching. Signing in with a KIIT account unlocks gender-filtered matching. Signing in upgrades the same account, so rooms and pseudonym carry over. Guest accounts inactive for 60 days are deleted.
rationale: Product principle: share something about yourself to use the same thing about others. Low friction to try the app, with accountability where it matters most.
tradeoffs: Guest accounts are cheap to create, so guest signup needs rate limits and a CAPTCHA. A guest who loses their browser session loses the account.

title: KIIT verification uses Google sign-in, checks the hd claim and keys accounts on sub
context: KIIT mail is hosted on Google Workspace (MX and SPF records point to Google). A test with a real KIIT account on 2026-10-02 signed in to an unpublished third-party app and returned hd=kiit.ac.in, email_verified=true and a token lifetime of 3600 seconds.
options: Google sign-in
Emailed one-time code
Third-party auth provider
decision: Verify the Google ID token, require hd == kiit.ac.in and email_verified, and store sub as the account's identity key.
rationale: Google states that hd must be checked when restricting access to a domain and that email should not be the primary identifier. No extra provider or email service is needed.
tradeoffs: Depends on KIIT continuing to allow third-party sign-in. The test ran while the app was in Testing status and must be repeated after publishing.

title: Gender is self-declared once after verification and only an admin can change it
context: Gender-filtered matching needs a gender. Reading it from the Google profile was considered.
options: Read gender from Google's People API
Self-declared in the app, changeable any time
Self-declared once, then locked
decision: After KIIT sign-in the user chooses male, female or prefer not to say. The choice is enforced as permanent by the server. Changes go through a request that an admin reviews. Users who prefer not to say cannot use the gender filter and are not counted in gender totals.
rationale: Gender is not in Google's ID token, and reading it needs an additional permission and API. A Google profile gender is user-editable too, so it is no more trustworthy. The real deterrent is that a ban follows the KIIT account.
tradeoffs: Relies on an admin process for corrections. Self-declared gender can be false.

title: No public admin interface in v1
context: Admin actions (reviewing reports, banning, approving gender changes) need a surface, and the code is public.
options: Admin web pages behind login
Admin command-line tool used from inside the cluster
decision: Admin actions run through a command-line tool that talks to the services inside the cluster. Nothing admin-related is reachable from the internet. Every admin action is recorded with who, what, when and why.
rationale: The smallest attack surface is having no admin endpoint to attack.
tradeoffs: Less convenient than a web page, and only people with cluster access can moderate.

title: The Google OAuth client lives in its own project with no billing account
context: When the trial ends, every project linked to the trial billing account is stopped.
options: OAuth client in the trial project
Separate project without billing
decision: The OAuth client is in a separate Google Cloud project (flamingo-auth) with no billing attached.
rationale: Sign-in keeps working after the trial ends and after the backend moves to another provider. Creating and using the client without billing was confirmed on 2026-10-02.
tradeoffs: One more project to manage.

title: v1 feature scope
context: The launch needs a scope small enough for the timeline and complete enough to be safe and worth returning to.
options: PRD phase 1 as written
PRD phase 1 plus safety at launch and a reason to return
decision: Accounts (guest, KIIT sign-in, one-time gender, new-device sign-in, change pseudonym); random and gender-filtered 1:1 matching with skip; group rooms with invite codes and one default campus room; live online counts; report and block with an admin queue and bans; saved group history; privacy policy and terms; mutual 'keep chatting' to turn a random chat into a saved conversation. Out: media, typing indicators, read receipts, push notifications, group search, profiles, native apps.
rationale: Report and block cannot wait for a later phase in an anonymous app. 'Keep chatting' addresses the drop-off after day two that ended the earlier prototype.
tradeoffs: A larger v1 than the original walking skeleton.

title: Project docs had drifted from the code
what_happened: CLAUDE.md stated that every module pins grpc v1.71.1. services/identity has required v1.74.2 since commit 8dcffcc, and in workspace mode every module therefore builds against v1.74.2. Comments in ci.yml pointed to knowledge-base paths that no longer existed.
impact: No build failure, but the documented state was wrong and could have misled a dependency change.
root_cause: The current-state section was maintained by hand and never checked against the code.
resolution: Every module's go.mod and go.work now require go 1.27.2 and google.golang.org/grpc v1.84.0, with golang.org/x/net, golang.org/x/text, github.com/jackc/pgx/v5 and github.com/go-jose/go-jose/v4 bumped to versions with no known vulnerabilities (govulncheck reports none, across every module, as of 2026-10-13). AGENTS.md and CONTRIBUTING.md now state the current version instead of a value nobody re-checks.
lessons: Check stated facts with a command before repeating them. Workspace mode picks one version per dependency for all modules.

title: Planning claims about outside products were made from memory and several were wrong
what_happened: During planning, statements about external products were made without checking. Examples: that RabbitMQ deletes every message once read (RabbitMQ Streams keep messages and support replay), a Google ID token lifetime that the docs do not state, and that Claude Code needs a pointer file to read AGENTS.md.
impact: Budget and architecture reasoning was briefly based on unverified statements.
root_cause: No rule required checking official documentation before stating external facts.
resolution: Every earlier claim was re-checked against official documentation and corrected or retracted. DEC-0017 makes verification a standing rule.
lessons: A plausible statement is not a verified one. Cite the source or label the claim unverified.

title: Identity checks the email suffix instead of the hd claim and keys verified accounts on email
what_happened: A review against Google's documentation found two gaps in VerifyBadge: it accepts any verified email ending in the college domain, and it treats the email as the unique identity.
impact: No known misuse; badge verification is not live yet.
root_cause: The first implementation predates reading Google's guidance. Google states the hd claim must be checked when restricting access to a domain, and that email should not be the primary identifier because it can change.
resolution: SignInWithGoogle (DEC-0056) checks strings.EqualFold(claims.HD, collegeDomain) and claims.EmailVerified, and keys every verified account on google_sub (DEC-0055), populated from the OIDC token's sub claim. VerifyBadge, which had the original gap, is removed entirely.
lessons: Read the provider's verification guidance before designing the check - confirmed again here as the right habit, since the fix was exactly what DEC-0027 had already specified once the guidance was read.

title: The web frontend lives in web/ and is hosted on Vercel
context: No frontend existed in the plan. The earlier prototype used a React-based frontend on Vercel calling a Go backend.
options: Serve the frontend from the cluster
Host it separately on Vercel
decision: The frontend is a separate app in web/ at the repo root, deployed to Vercel's free Hobby plan and calling the gateway. The framework is still to be chosen.
rationale: A familiar setup at no cost, and the frontend address does not change when the backend moves. The Hobby plan is limited to non-commercial use, which fits.
tradeoffs: Cross-origin requests need configuration at the gateway. Hobby plan limits apply.

title: Use a neutral project domain, not the maintainer's personal domain
context: Google sign-in requires an HTTPS origin that is not a raw IP address, and Google's brand verification requires DNS-level proof of domain ownership. The maintainer owns a personal domain but does not want their name in the app's address.
options: Subdomain of the personal domain
Only a vercel.app address
A separate project domain
decision: Use a domain named after the project. Order of preference: a free first-year domain from the GitHub Student Developer Pack, a domain bought at cost from Cloudflare Registrar, a free subdomain service as a last resort. The name is not chosen yet.
rationale: A domain you control gives HTTPS for frontend and backend, brand verification, and links that survive a migration.
tradeoffs: A possible renewal cost after the first year.

title: Commits and pull request descriptions carry no AI attribution
context: Claude Code adds a Co-Authored-By trailer to commits by default. The first commit of the repository and the repository-foundation commit both carried one. The maintainer does not want AI co-authorship recorded in the history.
options: Keep the default trailer
Remove it from new commits only
Remove it from new commits and from the existing history
decision: No commit message or pull request description credits an AI tool. .claude/settings.json sets attribution.commit and attribution.pr to empty strings, and AGENTS.md states the rule for other tools. The existing history was rewritten on 2026-10-03 to remove the trailer from the first commit, and main was force-pushed.
rationale: The maintainer's rule for this repository. A setting enforces it for Claude Code and a written rule covers every other tool and contributor.
tradeoffs: Rewriting the first commit changed the hash of every commit. Commit hashes recorded before 2026-10-03 no longer exist on main, and any earlier clone must be re-cloned or reset.

title: The project is licensed under Apache 2.0
context: The repository was public with no license, so nobody else could legally copy, modify or distribute the code, and it was not open source in practice.
options: MIT
Apache 2.0
AGPL 3.0
decision: License the project under the Apache License, Version 2.0. The LICENSE file holds the unmodified text from apache.org.
rationale: A permissive license that lets anyone use, change and share the code, with an explicit patent grant from contributors and a requirement to state changes. Contributions are licensed under the same terms by section 5 of the license.
tradeoffs: Others may run modified copies without publishing their changes, which AGPL 3.0 would have required. Slightly more conditions than MIT.

title: Live delivery goes only through Redis pub/sub; streaming gRPC for room events is removed
context: docs/SYSTEM_DESIGN.md and chat.proto described two mechanisms for getting a message to a connected client: Redis pub/sub between gateway instances, and a StreamRoomEvents gRPC call. Only one was ever going to be built.
options: Redis pub/sub only
Streaming gRPC only
Keep both
decision: The gateway subscribes to Redis channels for rooms it has local clients in. StreamRoomEvents is removed from chat.proto in the protocol redesign.
rationale: One mechanism is simpler to build, test and reason about, and scales the same way regardless of how many gateway instances are running.
tradeoffs: Redis pub/sub is at-most-once (see DEC-0015); a disconnected client must reload history rather than resume a stream.

title: Chat messages and user-facing events go to Kafka only; workers fan out to Redis and Postgres
context: DEC-0020 chose Kafka as the durable path but left open whether a service also writes to Redis directly on the way to recording the event.
options: Producer writes Kafka only, workers fan out
Producer writes Kafka then Redis itself
Producer writes Redis and Kafka at the same time
decision: Chat, Matching and Moderation produce only to Kafka. A delivery worker consumes and publishes to Redis for live delivery; a persistence worker consumes and writes to Postgres.
rationale: Kafka is the single entry point, so nothing is ever shown live that was not durably recorded, and each concern (live delivery, durable storage) scales and fails independently.
tradeoffs: One extra network hop between a message being sent and a client seeing it, compared to publishing to Redis directly.

title: No streaming gRPC calls between services
context: matching.proto's RequestMatch and chat.proto's StreamRoomEvents were the only streaming RPCs. A long-lived stream ties a waiting client to one instance of the service it is streaming from.
options: Keep streaming RPCs
Replace with unary calls plus Redis for anything that arrives later
decision: Every internal gRPC call is a plain request and response. A result that arrives later, such as a match being found, reaches the user through their own Redis channel instead.
rationale: Services can scale and restart independently of which instance a client happened to connect to, and pkg/grpclog's request logging covers every call without a separate streaming interceptor.
tradeoffs: An extra Redis round trip for anything that used to arrive over an open stream.

title: Local development runs on Tilt with a local kind cluster; docker-compose is retired
context: Local development needs the same services, soon including Kafka, and the production target is Kubernetes on Google Cloud (DEC-0023). docker-compose only exercises Postgres, Redis and (until now) RabbitMQ as plain containers, not as Kubernetes workloads.
options: Keep docker-compose
Tilt against a local kind cluster
Tilt against a shared remote cluster
decision: Tilt runs every service and its dependencies on a local kind cluster inside Docker, using the same Kubernetes manifests and Helm chart that deploy to Google Cloud.
rationale: The same files are exercised locally and in production, so a manifest bug shows up before it reaches the cluster that costs money. A local cluster is free and needs no image registry, unlike a remote one.
tradeoffs: More moving parts than docker-compose, and a new tool to learn.

title: The web app is a React, Vite and TypeScript single-page app
context: docs/PLAN.md listed the frontend framework as an open planning question.
options: React with Vite
Next.js
decision: A React + Vite + TypeScript single-page app in web/, deployed to Vercel.
rationale: The backend is Go and serves JSON and WebSocket frames; a single-page app needs none of a framework like Next.js's server-side rendering or API routes, and Vite's dev server starts faster for a straightforward app of this size.
tradeoffs: No server-side rendering, which this app does not need anyway since every page requires a signed-in or guest session.

title: Move the project to the Go version actually installed, and keep it current
context: DEC-0010 pinned dependencies to versions the installed Go 1.24.3 toolchain could build, because the network could not reliably fetch a newer toolchain at the time. The maintainer's machine now has Go 1.27.1 installed, and Go 1.27.2 is the current stable release.
options: Keep the Go 1.24.3 pin
Move to whatever Go version is currently installed and current
decision: Every go.work and go.mod file now declares go 1.27.2, the current stable release, with GOTOOLCHAIN=local kept in CI so a version mismatch fails fast rather than triggering a download.
rationale: govulncheck found Go standard library vulnerabilities fixed only in 1.27.2 (security fixes to net/http, crypto/tls and other packages, per the Go 1.27.2 release notes), on top of grpc, golang.org/x/net, golang.org/x/text, pgx and go-jose vulnerabilities fixed only in newer releases. Dependencies may now use current versions instead of ones held back to support an old Go version.
tradeoffs: The pinned version will drift behind upstream again and needs periodic review, same as DEC-0010's original tradeoff.

title: Branch protection requires one summary CI job, not every individual check
context: CI is gaining several jobs (build and test, lint, vulnerability scan, decision log check), each running once per module as a matrix. Naming every matrix combination as a required status check means editing branch protection every time a module or a job is added.
options: List every job and matrix combination as a required check
One summary job that depends on all the others
decision: A ci-ok job needs every other job and fails if any of them failed or were cancelled. Branch protection requires only ci-ok.
rationale: Adding a module or a CI job never requires a branch protection change to go with it.
tradeoffs: A failure in any underlying job is reported through ci-ok, one step removed from the job that actually failed, so a quick skim means opening the workflow run rather than reading the required-checks list alone.

title: One sign-in RPC covers new, returning and upgrading accounts; sessions are a self-signed JWT
context: DEC-0026 and DEC-0027 set the account tiers and verification method, but not the mechanics: what RPC a client calls, what the gateway's own session token looks like, and how a banned account is kept out.
options: A session store in Redis, looked up per request
A self-signed JWT, checked against a Redis ban set
Separate RPCs for sign-up, sign-in and upgrade
decision: Identity.SignInWithGoogle(id_token, guest_account_id?) covers all three cases (existing verified account, upgrading a guest, creating new) in one call. The gateway signs its own session JWT (HMAC-SHA256, 60-day lifetime, refreshed if older than 24 hours on WebSocket auth) and holds no tier or gender in its claims, so a permission change takes effect on the account's next connection rather than needing the token itself revoked.
rationale: One RPC is simpler for the gateway to call than branching client-side on which case applies. A stateless JWT needs no session store; revocation goes through the existing banned-accounts set instead of a separate deny-list.
tradeoffs: A stolen token is valid for its full lifetime unless the account is banned; there is no way to revoke one token without banning the account.

title: A versioned JSON HTTP API plus a typed WebSocket frame protocol, both under the gateway
context: Nothing had defined what the browser actually sends and receives - the RPC redesign (DEC-0038) assumes a concrete client-facing protocol to translate into those calls.
options: GraphQL
A single WebSocket connection for everything, including one-shot actions
JSON over HTTPS for one-shot actions, a separate WebSocket for anything live
decision: One-shot actions (sign-in, room management, history) are plain JSON over HTTPS under /v1. Live interaction (sending messages, matching, presence) runs over one WebSocket per client, with every frame a JSON object carrying a type field.
rationale: This is the same split gateway.md already described for HTTP versus WebSocket; writing out the exact paths and frame types now is what actually lets the frontend and gateway be built against the same contract without guessing at each other's shape.
tradeoffs: Two protocols to keep in sync by hand, since neither is generated from a shared schema the way the gRPC contracts are.

title: Three Kafka topics, protobuf envelopes, no schema registry
context: DEC-0020 and DEC-0037 chose Kafka as the durable path but not the topic layout or how a consumer knows what shape an event is.
options: One topic per event type
One topic per owning service, with an envelope oneof
A shared schema registry
decision: chat.events, matching.events and moderation.events, each keyed for the ordering that topic needs (room, room, account). Each message is a protobuf envelope with a oneof over that topic's event kinds, defined in a new proto/events/v1 package versioned in this repository.
rationale: One topic per service keeps related events (a room's messages and its membership changes) in order on one partition, which one topic per event type would not. Versioning payloads as repository-tracked .proto files, the same way gRPC contracts already are, is one less moving part than running a schema registry at this scale.
tradeoffs: A consumer that only cares about one event kind still receives the whole topic and filters client-side.

title: Matching uses one atomic Redis script over a bounded candidate window, not a queue per preference pair
context: The match queue has to be fast, fair, and never pair two people who shouldn't be paired (blocked, previous partner, incompatible preference) - and the prior design only sketched the queue's existence, not how a match is actually found without a race between two users matching the same third person.
options: A database table with row locking
A separate queue per (preference, gender) combination
One Lua script run atomically in Redis over a bounded candidate scan
decision: RequestMatch runs one Redis script that scans the oldest 100 waiting entries for a compatible match; if none, the caller is enqueued. Entries older than 10 minutes are dropped. Compatibility excludes blocks and immediate repeat pairings.
rationale: A single atomic script removes the race condition without needing a separate lock; capping the scan at 100 keeps it fast regardless of queue size, which is enough at pilot scale.
tradeoffs: A queue deeper than 100 waiting users could fail to find a compatible match that exists further back, until older entries expire; acceptable for a pilot, worth revisiting if the queue ever gets that deep.

title: Presence counts come from batched heartbeats into Redis sorted sets, published every 5 seconds
context: presence.proto already defined a Heartbeat RPC, but not its frequency, batching, or how a disconnected client's count gets removed without an explicit sign-off call.
options: A heartbeat per connection, per interval
One batched heartbeat per gateway instance, aged out of a sorted set
decision: Each gateway sends one Heartbeat covering all its connections every 15 seconds. Presence keeps a Redis sorted set per category, scored by last-heartbeat time, drops entries older than 45 seconds, and publishes totals every 5 seconds.
rationale: Batching means the number of Heartbeat calls doesn't grow with the number of connected users, only with the number of gateway instances. Aging out of a sorted set needs no explicit disconnect handling - a crashed gateway's users simply age out within 45 seconds.
tradeoffs: A count can be briefly stale (up to 45 seconds) after a client disconnects without a clean close.

title: Reports are stored and queued; blocks are enforced at match time and client-side in groups; bans propagate through a Redis set and a forced disconnect
context: DEC-0029 and DEC-0031 established that reports go to an admin queue and that blocking exists, but not the mechanics of how a block actually stops two people from being matched again, or how a ban takes effect on an already-connected session.
options: Bans checked only at the next sign-in
Bans enforced immediately via a Redis set every gateway already checks, plus a forced disconnect
decision: A report is stored and produces a ReportFiled event. A block adds each account to the other's avoid set, which Matching reads, and ends their current random chat. A ban adds the account to a Redis banned set, produces an event the delivery worker turns into a kicked frame, and every gateway checks the set on sign-in, on connect and on every send.
rationale: Checking a widely-read Redis set on the hot path is cheap, and it means a ban takes effect within the delivery worker's lag rather than waiting for the user's session to end on its own.
tradeoffs: Three separate places check the banned set (sign-in, connect, send); missing one in a future change would let a banned user act until their connection drops.

title: At-least-once delivery everywhere Kafka is involved, made safe with idempotent writes; dependency outages degrade delivery speed, not correctness
context: Nothing had said what happens when Kafka, Redis or Postgres is unreachable, or what delivery guarantee a consumer can assume - needed before writing any consumer, since it decides whether writes have to be idempotent.
options: Exactly-once delivery via transactional writes
At-most-once, accepting occasional message loss
At-least-once, with consumers that tolerate replays
decision: Consumers commit their Kafka offset only after finishing their work, giving at-least-once delivery. Writes are idempotent (message ids are the primary key; duplicate inserts are no-ops) so a replay after a crash doesn't duplicate data. On an outage, the affected path queues up and catches up afterward rather than losing or duplicating data; SendMessage itself fails loudly if Kafka is unreachable, rather than showing a message that was never recorded.
rationale: Exactly-once delivery across Kafka, Redis and Postgres together isn't practical at this scale without a distributed transaction, which is far more complexity than the failure actually justifies here.
tradeoffs: A consumer that crashes after finishing its work but before committing the offset reprocesses that message once more - harmless given idempotent writes, but worth knowing when reading a consumer's logs.

title: Unit tests against fakes, integration tests against real dependencies behind a build tag, and one end-to-end smoke test over the real protocol
context: Identity's test approach (fakes only) doesn't exercise a Kafka consumer, a Redis script, or the WebSocket protocol end to end, and those are exactly the parts new in this design most likely to have a bug that only shows up against the real thing (INC-0003 already found one database-specific bug fakes couldn't catch).
options: Fakes only, as Identity does now
Fakes for business logic, integration tests behind a build tag for storage and broker code, plus one end-to-end smoke test
decision: Business logic keeps using in-memory fakes. Code that talks to Postgres, Redis or Kafka directly also gets a test behind the integration build tag, run against the real thing in the local Tilt cluster. One Go module, tests/e2e, drives the gateway's real HTTP and WebSocket surface through the flows in the PRD (match, chat, keep, group room, report, block, ban).
rationale: This is the same lesson INC-0003 already taught Identity, extended to the services that now talk to a broker as well as a database. The end-to-end test is the only thing that actually proves the full chain (gateway to Kafka to worker to Redis to gateway to client) works together.
tradeoffs: Integration and end-to-end tests need the local cluster running and are slower than unit tests; they aren't yet wired into CI (open question in docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §13).

title: A development-only fake Google verifier, enabled by an explicit environment variable
context: Verified-account flows need a Google ID token to test, but getting a real one needs a browser and a real sign-in, which a backend test or an automated end-to-end run can't do.
options: Test only against the real Google verifier, by hand
A development-only verifier that accepts a fabricated but clearly-marked token format
decision: With DEV_FAKE_GOOGLE=1, Identity accepts tokens shaped like fake:<sub>:<email> instead of a real Google-signed JWT. It logs a warning on startup and is never the default.
rationale: This is what actually makes the verified-account path testable in the end-to-end suite and by hand during local development, without needing a browser in the loop or real Google credentials in a test environment.
tradeoffs: A real Google ID token is never exercised locally; DEC-0027's test on the real KIIT flow stays the only check against the real provider, and must be repeated once sign-in is published to production.

title: Two new services: a delivery worker and an admin command-line tool
context: DEC-0037 (Kafka-only, workers fan out) and DEC-0029 (no public admin surface) both imply a piece of code that didn't exist in the original seven-service list.
options: Fold delivery into the persistence worker
A separate delivery-worker service
A separate tool rather than a service for admin actions
decision: delivery-worker is its own Go module, consuming every topic and publishing to Redis, with no state of its own. tools/admin is a command-line program, not a long-running service, that calls Moderation and Identity from inside the cluster.
rationale: A separate delivery worker can be scaled and restarted independently of the persistence worker, and a failure writing to Postgres never blocks live delivery or the reverse. An admin tool that is a command, not a service, has nothing listening on a port to ever expose by accident.
tradeoffs: One more Go module to build, test and deploy.

title: Implementation choices for the local Tilt environment: distroless images, emptyDir storage, no local registry yet
context: DEC-0039 already chose Tilt on a local kind cluster. Building it out needed several concrete choices DEC-0039 did not cover: what base image each service's Dockerfile ends on, whether local Postgres/Redis/Kafka get a PersistentVolumeClaim, and whether to add ctlptl for a local image registry.
options: gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12:nonroot vs. alpine vs. scratch for the runtime image
emptyDir vs. a PersistentVolumeClaim for Postgres/Redis/Kafka data
Plain kind (Tilt falls back to `kind load docker-image`) vs. ctlptl with a local registry
decision: Every service's final image is gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12:nonroot, confirmed by inspecting the image directly (not assumed from its docs) to carry CA certificates and a non-root user. Postgres, Redis and Kafka all use emptyDir, not a PVC. Tilt uses the plain `kind load` fallback; ctlptl and a local registry are not set up.
rationale: Every service already builds as a static CGO_ENABLED=0 binary (confirmed for identity, the most dependency-heavy service), so distroless/static needs nothing else and is as small an attack surface as an image can have. This local cluster is recreated from scratch regularly (`kind delete cluster`), so a PVC would not actually survive that either - emptyDir is honest about that and needs no StorageClass. `kind load` is slower than a local registry but needs one less tool; Tilt's own docs recommend ctlptl mainly for larger teams, which this project is not.
tradeoffs: Every pod restart loses its data, which is correct for local development but would be wrong to carry into the real deployment. Image rebuilds are slower than they would be with a local registry - worth revisiting with ctlptl if that becomes an annoyance.

title: A single transient module-proxy failure cancelled 8 unrelated CI jobs
what_happened: On PR #6, build-and-test (services/presence) failed to download golang.org/x/text@v0.42.0 from proxy.golang.org (an HTTP/2 stream error on Google's own proxy, not a real problem with the dependency or its version). Every other build-and-test matrix job was immediately cancelled as a result, because strategy.fail-fast defaults to true: one matrix entry failing cancels the rest of that matrix.
impact: A one-off network blip looked like nine failing jobs instead of one, and would have needed re-running the whole matrix instead of just the one that actually failed.
root_cause: fail-fast was left at its GitHub Actions default (true) on all three matrix strategies (build-and-test, lint, vulncheck).
resolution: Set fail-fast: false on all three. A real failure in one module no longer hides or cancels the result for every other module.
lessons: A proxy.golang.org download failure is a transient infrastructure issue to re-run, not a reason to doubt the dependency versions - check the actual error text before assuming a real bug. Matrix CI jobs that are meant to report independently (one status per module) need fail-fast: false explicitly; the default optimizes for 'stop early', not 'tell me about every module'.

title: Protocol redesign implemented: one Request/Response type per RPC, a new events package, VerifyBadge kept one PR longer
context: docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §5.3 and §5.4 described the gRPC and Kafka contract changes needed before Gateway, Chat and Matching could be built, but not the concrete message shapes. Writing them surfaced two things the design hadn't settled: every RPC needs its own uniquely-named request and response message to pass buf's STANDARD lint rules (the previous contracts shared message types across RPCs and failed this, per DEC-0036 to DEC-0038's context), and literally removing VerifyBadge now, as §5.3 says, would break Identity's existing compiled and tested implementation in a pull request that is only supposed to touch contracts.
options: Share message types across RPCs where the shape matches (the old style)
One Request/Response type per RPC, matching buf's STANDARD lint rules
Remove VerifyBadge now and also strip its implementation and tests in this PR
Keep VerifyBadge and its implementation until the PR that adds SignInWithGoogle removes both together
decision: Every RPC across identity, chat, matching, presence and moderation now has its own <Method>Request/<Method>Response message. A new proto/events/v1/events.proto defines the three Kafka envelopes from DEC-0043 (ChatEvent, MatchingEvent, ModerationEvent), each a oneof over its topic's event kinds; it declares no RPCs, so none of buf's RPC naming rules apply to it. VerifyBadge stays in identity.proto, marked deprecated, with Identity's server.go updated only enough to keep compiling against the new wrapped response types - its removal, and SignInWithGoogle's implementation, are the next pull request's job.
rationale: buf lint now passes cleanly (confirmed: zero issues), which is what lets buf breaking be turned on for every pull request after this one. Keeping VerifyBadge one PR longer means this pull request changes only contracts, as planned, instead of also rewriting Identity's service logic; its own tests keep passing unmodified except for the mechanical response-wrapping change every existing RPC needed.
tradeoffs: identity.proto briefly carries one deprecated RPC with real callers alongside the new ones with none yet. buf breaking could not be turned on in this same pull request - it would fail against its own base, since this redesign is intentionally breaking - so it is enabled in the immediate follow-up instead, once this lands on main.

title: Migration 0002 keys verified accounts on google_sub, drops badge_verified, adds last_seen_at
context: DEC-0027 and DEC-0041 decided accounts should be keyed on Google's sub claim and that SignInWithGoogle needs to tell new, returning and upgraded accounts apart, and DEC-0026's guest cleanup needs a timestamp to measure inactivity against. The existing schema only had a boolean badge_verified with no room for any of this.
options: Keep badge_verified and add the new columns alongside it
Replace badge_verified with a nullable google_sub (NULL means not linked) plus gender_set_at and last_seen_at
decision: Migration 0002 adds google_sub TEXT UNIQUE, gender_set_at TIMESTAMPTZ and last_seen_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(), and drops badge_verified. Verification status is now derived from google_sub being non-null rather than stored twice.
rationale: A nullable unique column does double duty as both the identity key for GetByGoogleSub and the verified/not-verified flag, so there is no way for the two to disagree the way a separate boolean could drift from the link. last_seen_at defaulting to now() means every existing row gets a sane value with no backfill step.
tradeoffs: The down migration cannot bring back badge_verified's old values, since they were never equivalent to google_sub being set - rolling back loses the distinction entirely. This is accepted because badge_verified was never live (INC-0006).

title: SignInWithGoogle resolved as a lookup-then-link-then-create chain, racing on LinkGoogle's unique constraint
context: DEC-0041 specified one RPC covering three cases (existing verified account, upgrading a guest, creating new), and INC-0006 required checking the hd claim and email_verified and keying on sub instead of email. Two sign-ins for the same Google account racing each other needed a defined outcome, not just a happy-path implementation.
options: Check-then-act: look up by sub, and if absent, assume no race and create or link
Try GetByGoogleSub, then try LinkGoogle (or CreateVerified with no guest id), and on a unique-constraint violation from a concurrent duplicate, re-fetch by sub instead of surfacing the error
decision: SignInWithGoogle rejects the token first (email_verified and strings.EqualFold(claims.HD, collegeDomain)), then tries GetByGoogleSub; on a miss it tries LinkGoogle against the supplied guest id (or CreateVerified with a generated pseudonym if there is none), and if that fails with store.ErrAlreadyExists - meaning another request linked the same sub first - it falls back to a second GetByGoogleSub rather than returning an error to the caller.
rationale: The database's unique constraint on google_sub (DEC-0055) is the actual source of truth for uniqueness; the race-safe fallback means two near-simultaneous sign-ins from the same Google account both succeed and return the same account, instead of one of them failing for a reason the client can't do anything about.
tradeoffs: Two code paths reach the same GetByGoogleSub call (the initial lookup and the race fallback), which is a small amount of duplication kept because unifying them into one retry loop made the happy path harder to read for a case that is rare in practice.

title: SetGender's once-only rule is enforced by the database, not just checked in the handler
context: DEC-0028 decided gender is self-declared once and only an admin can change it afterward. A handler-level check alone (read gender_set_at, then write if null) has a race window between the read and the write.
options: Check gender_set_at in the handler before writing, with no database-level guarantee
A single conditional UPDATE (... WHERE gender_set_at IS NULL) as the only way gender is ever set, with a follow-up Get to tell 'not found' apart from 'already set' when it matches zero rows
decision: Postgres.SetGender runs one conditional UPDATE. If it affects zero rows, a follow-up Get determines whether the account doesn't exist (ErrNotFound) or exists with gender already set (the new ErrAlreadySet sentinel). AdminSetGender uses a separate, unconditional UPDATE with no such guard, since DEC-0028 allows an admin to change it at any time.
rationale: The conditional UPDATE is atomic, so two concurrent SetGender calls for the same account can't both succeed - confirmed by TestPostgresSetGenderOnceEnforcedByTheDatabase against a real database, not just the in-memory fake (INC-0003's lesson applied here directly).
tradeoffs: Zero rows affected is ambiguous on its own, so every SetGender call that hits zero rows costs a second round trip to disambiguate. Accepted since SetGender is called once per account's lifetime in the normal case, not on a hot path.

title: A generated two-word pseudonym for accounts created directly by SignInWithGoogle
context: Most verified accounts come from upgrading an existing guest, which already has a pseudonym. SignInWithGoogle's case C (no guest account supplied) has no existing pseudonym to carry over and still needs one to create the account with.
options: Require the client to always pass a guest_account_id, even if it has to create a throwaway guest first just to get a pseudonym
Generate a pseudonym server-side from a fixed adjective/noun word list
decision: generatePseudonym picks one of 30 adjectives and one of 30 nouns with math/rand/v2 and joins them, e.g. 'Silent Otter'. The caller retries on a collision rather than the generator checking uniqueness itself.
rationale: Requiring a guest account first would make case C pointless to have as a direct path at all. 900 combinations is enough given how few sign-ins are expected to skip the guest step (ARCHITECTURE §4.2), and collision retry is already how account creation handles the far more likely pseudonym collisions from the existing random-pseudonym generator used for new guests.
tradeoffs: math/rand/v2 is not cryptographically secure, which golangci-lint's gosec flagged (G404); suppressed with a //nolint:gosec comment explaining that a display name has no security requirement for unpredictability.

title: cleanup-guests runs as a CronJob invoking the same binary in a different mode, not a separate service
context: DEC-0026's guest accounts need periodic deletion once inactive, which needs something to trigger on a schedule. Kubernetes CronJobs are the natural fit, but that still leaves the question of what image and command the CronJob runs.
options: A separate small service or script, with its own image and Dockerfile, built and deployed independently of identity
identity's own binary, dispatching on os.Args[1] == "cleanup-guests" to run the deletion once and exit instead of starting the gRPC server
An HTTP or gRPC endpoint on identity itself, triggered by an external scheduler
decision: main.go checks os.Args[1] before anything else; "cleanup-guests" runs connectAndMigrate, calls store.DeleteStaleGuests once, logs the count, and exits, while anything else falls through to the normal server. deploy/helm/service's new cronjob.yaml (guarded by a cronJob value block, used by identity's values.yaml with schedule 17 3 * * * and args ["cleanup-guests"]) runs this against the exact same image the Deployment uses.
rationale: Reusing identity's image means the CronJob can never drift out of sync with the Deployment's schema assumptions or store code - there is only one build to keep correct. The schedule is off the hour (3:17 AM) specifically to avoid a thundering herd with other jobs that default to the hour or midnight.
tradeoffs: identity's main.go now has two execution modes instead of one, which a reader has to notice before assuming main() always starts a server. deploy/helm/service's chart gained a conditional template that every other service's values.yaml simply doesn't set.

title: Identity's new store methods get integration tests against a real Postgres, following DEC-0048
context: DEC-0048 already decided storage code gets integration-tagged tests against the real database in addition to fakes. Identity's store package gained several guarantees in this change - SetGender's once-only enforcement, Touch's write throttle, uniqueness on google_sub - that are specifically about what Postgres does, not what the fake does.
options: Extend the existing fakes with the same logic the real store has and trust that they match
A //go:build integration test file exercising the real Postgres.* methods directly, run manually against a local database (not yet wired into CI)
decision: postgres_integration_test.go adds 7 tests covering create/get, a malformed-id lookup, LinkGoogle plus GetByGoogleSub, LinkGoogle's duplicate-sub rejection, SetGender's once-only enforcement, Touch's throttle window, and DeleteStaleGuests leaving fresh guests and verified accounts alone. Each test connects to POSTGRES_URL (defaulting to the local Tilt instance), runs migrations, and truncates accounts for isolation.
rationale: A fake that reimplements SetGender's conditional-UPDATE race safety would just be asserting the fake agrees with itself, not that Postgres actually enforces it - this is exactly the gap INC-0003 already identified. Running these against a real throwaway container (verified passing before merging) confirmed the queries are correct against actual Postgres semantics, not just the mental model of them.
tradeoffs: These tests need a real Postgres and are not part of the normal `go test ./...` run (the integration build tag excludes them by default), so they can be forgotten; DEC-0048 already flagged wiring integration tests into CI as an open question.

title: Kafka and Redis Go client libraries: IBM/sarama and redis/go-redis/v9
context: T6 needed a Kafka producer and a Redis client for Chat, and DEC-0020/DEC-0037 chose Kafka and Redis without picking concrete libraries. The build plan called for verifying the choice, not assuming one from memory (AGENTS.md rule 1).
options: segmentio/kafka-go for Kafka
IBM/sarama for Kafka
confluent-kafka-go (cgo wrapper around librdkafka) for Kafka
redis/go-redis/v9 for Redis (the only serious pure-Go option)
decision: github.com/IBM/sarama v1.61.1 for Kafka, github.com/redis/go-redis/v9 v9.23.0 for Redis.
rationale: Checked each candidate's actual repository state rather than trusting memory: segmentio/kafka-go's last release and last commit were both from April 2026, six months stale as of this decision, while sarama released v1.61.1 in September 2026 and had commits the day before this check. sarama's own source (its KafkaVersion list) explicitly names V4_3_1_0 as supported, an exact match for the apache/kafka:4.3.1 this project runs (deploy/k8s/dev/kafka.yaml). confluent-kafka-go needs cgo and librdkafka, which conflicts with every service's CGO_ENABLED=0 distroless build (DEC-0053). Both libraries' go.mod files declare go 1.26.0, compatible with this project's 1.27.2 (DEC-0051).
tradeoffs: sarama's API is lower-level than kafka-go's in places (no built-in reader abstraction), meaning the delivery worker and persistence worker will need their own small amount of consumer-group boilerplate when they're built.

title: SendMessage's client_msg_id dedup lives in Redis, not Postgres, because Chat never writes messages itself
context: docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §3.1 and DEC-0047 establish that Chat's SendMessage only produces a MessageSent event to Kafka and never writes to the messages table itself - the persistence worker does that, asynchronously. The chat.proto comment on client_msg_id says a retried send 'is never recorded twice', but with nothing written to Postgres synchronously, there was nothing obvious to check a retry against.
options: Have SendMessage write a row to Postgres itself before producing to Kafka, so a unique constraint catches a retry
An in-memory, per-process map (no durability, lost on restart or across replicas)
A Redis key per (room, sender, client_msg_id), claimed with SETNX, holding the assigned message_id and sent_at
decision: internal/dedup.Deduper, backed by Redis SETNX with a 5-minute TTL. SendMessage generates a candidate message id, calls Claim, and on a losing claim (a retry) returns the winning claim's stored result instead of producing a second Kafka event.
rationale: Writing to Postgres synchronously would contradict the already-agreed sequence diagram in §3.1, which shows Chat producing to Kafka and returning without touching the database. Chat already depends on Redis for other things (the services table in §2 lists it), so this adds no new dependency. A 5-minute window is generous for any realistic client retry without accumulating keys forever.
tradeoffs: Redis is not durable by default in this local setup (no AOF/RDB persistence configured), so a Redis restart during the dedup window could theoretically let a retry through as a new message. Accepted as a low-probability, low-severity gap - a duplicate message is a client-visible nuisance, not data corruption, and is itself rarer than the retry it is meant to guard against.

title: Invite codes are generated with crypto/rand, not math/rand/v2
context: DEC-0058 (identity's pseudonym generator) deliberately used math/rand/v2 and suppressed golangci-lint's gosec warning, reasoning that a display name's predictability isn't a security concern. CreateGroupRoom and RotateInviteCode needed a similar random-string generator for invite codes, which is a different kind of value.
options: Reuse the same math/rand/v2 approach as the pseudonym generator, for consistency
crypto/rand, accepting the small extra cost of a cryptographically secure source
decision: generateInviteCode uses crypto/rand, drawing 8 characters from a 32-character alphabet that excludes easily-confused characters (0/O, 1/I/l).
rationale: Unlike a pseudonym, an invite code is a bearer credential - anyone who has it can join a private group room - so an attacker who could predict or narrow down the random source could guess working invite codes. That is exactly the kind of case DEC-0058's own reasoning said math/rand/v2 was fine to use BECAUSE it didn't apply; here it does apply, so the two generators deliberately use different random sources for different reasons, not by oversight.
tradeoffs: None of real consequence - crypto/rand is not meaningfully slower for generating 8 bytes, and this is not a hot path.

title: CreateDirectRoom produces no chat.events event; Matching's MatchFound covers it
context: chat.events' event list (MessageSent, MemberJoined, MemberLeft, KeepVote, RoomKept, RoomEnded) includes MemberJoined, and CreateDirectRoom does add both participants as members, so it was not obvious whether creating a direct room should also emit MemberJoined events the way JoinRoomByCode does.
options: Emit a MemberJoined event per participant when CreateDirectRoom runs, for consistency with JoinRoomByCode
Emit nothing - rely on Matching's own MatchFound event (matching.events, not yet built) to tell the delivery worker about the new room
decision: CreateDirectRoom does not publish to chat.events. It is called only by Matching (DEC-0044), never by a client, and docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §3.2 already has Matching producing MatchFound once it calls CreateDirectRoom.
rationale: A MemberJoined event here would tell the delivery worker the same fact MatchFound already tells it - that this room now exists with these two members - through a second, differently-shaped event for the same instant. Two sources of truth for one fact is exactly the kind of redundancy worth avoiding before it causes a consumer to have to reconcile them.
tradeoffs: This makes CreateDirectRoom's behavior non-obvious by just reading chat.events' event list; the reasoning lives here and in a comment on the handler, not in the proto itself.

title: RemoveMember currently only authorizes the room owner; the admin tool's ban path is deferred
context: docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §5.3 says RemoveMember covers both 'the owner removing someone, or the admin tool acting on a ban', but chat.proto's RemoveMemberRequest has only requested_by_account_id with no field distinguishing the two callers, and tools/admin does not exist yet (T9).
options: Guess at an admin bypass now (e.g. a magic account id or an unauthenticated internal flag) before the admin tool exists to define what it actually needs
Authorize only the room-owner case now, and extend this RPC (or add a field) when tools/admin is actually built
decision: RemoveMember returns PermissionDenied unless requested_by_account_id matches the room's owner. The admin-tool case is left unimplemented, called out in a comment on the handler, rather than designed against a tool that doesn't exist yet.
rationale: Designing an authorization bypass for a caller that isn't built yet risks guessing wrong about what tools/admin will actually look like (does it reach Chat directly, through Moderation, with what credential) and shipping a security-relevant mechanism nobody has reviewed. The owner-only path fully serves what's actually usable today.
tradeoffs: Until tools/admin lands, there is no way to remove a banned user from a group room they already belong to except asking the owner.

title: Chat's migrations collided with identity's because every service shares one Postgres database and golang-migrate's default tracking table
what_happened: Deploying Chat's T6 PR against the same local Postgres identity already uses, Chat's own migrations.Run() failed with 'no migration found for version 2: read down for version 2'. golang-migrate's pgx driver defaults its bookkeeping table to a fixed name, schema_migrations, in the public schema. Identity had already advanced that table to version 2 (its own migrations 0001 and 0002); Chat's migration source only goes up to 0001, so golang-migrate saw a recorded version higher than anything Chat's own source tree could explain and refused to proceed. Separately, Chat's Helm values never set POSTGRES_URL, so it was also falling back to its own code default of a localhost connection string instead of the in-cluster postgres service, the same oversight identity.yaml had already correctly avoided.
impact: Chat could not start against the shared local Postgres once identity had also run its migrations first - this would have affected every future service with its own migrations the moment two of them ran against the same database, not just Chat. Caught during this session's own live verification (a real kind cluster deployment) before being discovered by the maintainer or in a real environment.
root_cause: docs/ARCHITECTURE.md's services table says each service 'owns' its own schema (identity schema, chat schema, and so on), but neither identity's nor chat's migrations.go ever actually configured golang-migrate to track its own version history separately - both used the library's untouched default, which is one global table shared by whoever connects to the database.
resolution: Both services' migrations.go now pass pgxmigrate.Config{MigrationsTable: "<service>_schema_migrations"}, giving each its own independent version-tracking table in the same database rather than creating separate Postgres schemas (a smaller, lower-risk change that solves the actual collision without needing to move already-created tables between schemas). Verified by running identity's migrations, then chat's migrations, against the same real Postgres instance and confirming both tracking tables and all expected tables exist with no error. Chat's values.yaml also gained explicit POSTGRES_URL, KAFKA_BROKERS and REDIS_URL overrides pointing at the in-cluster service names, matching identity's existing pattern.
lessons: A fix verified only against a fresh, single-service database (as T5's integration tests were) can still hide a bug that only appears once a second service with its own migrations shares the same database - exactly the scenario this session's live, full kind-cluster deployment (not just `go test`) caught. Every future service with its own migrations needs this same explicit MigrationsTable setting from the start, not discovered the same way again.

title: The shared Helm chart gains a "worker" protocol for services with no server of their own
context: delivery-worker is a pure Kafka consumer with no gRPC or HTTP surface at all (DEC-0050), but deploy/helm/service's deployment.yaml and service.yaml templates assumed every service exposes some port and gets checked with either a gRPC or an HTTP readiness/liveness probe - there was no third option.
options: Give delivery-worker a throwaway HTTP server just to answer /healthz, purely to fit the existing grpc/http split
Extend the chart with a third protocol value, "worker", that skips the Service object, the container's ports, and both probes entirely
decision: protocol: worker renders a bare Deployment: no Service, no ports, no readinessProbe/livenessProbe. A crashed consumer process exits non-zero, which the Deployment's restartPolicy already handles without a probe's help.
rationale: A /healthz endpoint that exists only to satisfy a probe, with no other purpose, is exactly the kind of thing worth not building - it would need its own router, its own "am I actually consuming" logic to be meaningful, or it would just always return 200 and prove nothing a crash wouldn't already prove by itself via the exit code.
tradeoffs: There is currently no active signal that a worker is actually consuming (stuck but not crashed) versus merely running - only that its process is alive. Acceptable for now; a real liveness signal for this case (e.g. a lag-based check) is a reasonable future addition if a worker is ever observed to hang without crashing.

title: delivery-worker's Kafka-to-Redis routing: republish verbatim, route matching.events' two cases differently
context: docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §5.5 lists Redis channels (room:{room_id}, user:{account_id}) and which kinds of event go to each, but not the exact routing rule for every event kind, nor what shape the Redis payload itself should be - gateway, the only future consumer of these channels, does not exist yet to define that contract from its side.
options: Invent a new, gateway-facing JSON wire format for the Redis payload
Republish the original protobuf bytes unchanged, so a future gateway decodes with the same proto/events/v1 package that produced them
Route every matching.events kind to room:{room_id}, including MatchFound

Route MatchFound to both accounts' user:{account_id} (bootstrapping them onto a room they don't know exists yet) and MatchEnded to room:{room_id} (both sides are already subscribed to the room by then)
decision: Every Redis payload is the original Kafka message's value, unmodified. chat.events always goes to room:{room_id}. matching.events' MatchFound goes to both account_id_a and account_id_b's user:{account_id}; MatchEnded goes to room:{room_id}. moderation.events' AccountBanned goes to user:{account_id} (the "kicked" signal); ReportFiled, UserBlocked and AccountUnbanned have no live-delivery target and are intentionally dropped, since none has a corresponding WebSocket message in ARCHITECTURE §5.2.
rationale: Reusing the exact proto/events/v1 schemas means there is no second wire format to keep in sync with the first, consistent with DEC-0043's "no schema registry, versioned in the repository" reasoning. MatchFound can't go to room:{room_id} because neither gateway has subscribed to that room yet - the room didn't exist before this event - so it has to reach each account through a channel their gateway is already listening on by construction (every connected account's gateway subscribes to user:{account_id} as soon as it connects).
tradeoffs: This routing logic is effectively an unwritten contract with a gateway that doesn't exist yet; if gateway's own design (T7) needs a different shape, this will need revisiting then, not before.

title: A malformed Kafka message is marked (skipped); a failed Redis publish is left unmarked (retried)
context: DEC-0047 established at-least-once delivery with idempotent writes, but delivery-worker's two failure modes aren't equivalent: a message that fails to even decode as a valid proto envelope will fail exactly the same way on every redelivery, while a failed Redis publish is often a transient outage that resolves on its own.
options: Never mark a message that errors, for either failure mode - simplest, but a single malformed message would block every later message on that partition forever (Kafka delivers a partition strictly in order)
Always mark a message that errors, for either failure mode - simplest, but masks a real Redis outage as silently dropped events instead of degraded delivery
Mark (skip) a decode/routing failure; leave unmarked (retry) a publish failure
decision: consumer.Handler marks a message immediately when router.Route* returns an error (logged, then skipped), and leaves a message unmarked when Publish returns an error (logged, left for redelivery on the next session).
rationale: A decode failure means the bytes are not a ChatEvent/MatchingEvent/ModerationEvent at all - something no amount of retrying fixes, since Chat/Matching/Moderation only ever produce well-formed instances of these exact types. A publish failure is the kind of dependency outage DEC-0047 already says should 'degrade delivery speed, not correctness' - exactly what leaving it unmarked achieves.
tradeoffs: A MatchFound event with two targets, where the first publish succeeds and the second fails, redelivers to both on retry - the first account's gateway would see it twice. Accepted: Redis pub/sub is not a durable store, a duplicate live notification is a redundant UI update at worst, and this needs one publish to fail right after another succeeds, which is already rare.

title: persistence-worker writes a structured messages row for MessageSent and a generic analytics.events log for every event kind on every topic
context: docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §2 says persistence-worker owns an 'analytics schema' and 'writes chat.messages', but not the actual shape of the analytics side, or whether MessageSent should be logged there too alongside its structured row.
options: Only write the structured messages row for MessageSent; skip an analytics entry for it (no duplication)

A generic analytics.events table (event_id, topic, event_kind, raw payload, occurred_at) that logs every event from all three topics uniformly, including MessageSent, in addition to MessageSent's own structured row
decision: Every event persistence-worker consumes - from chat.events, matching.events and moderation.events alike - gets one row in analytics.events, keyed by event_id so a Kafka redelivery is a no-op insert. MessageSent additionally gets its own row in Chat's messages table, which is the only one any RPC (ListMessages) actually reads back.
rationale: A uniform log across every event kind is what makes a simple analytics query - counts per event kind per day, for instance - actually simple: no special-casing one kind as present in one table and absent from another. The duplication for MessageSent (both its own row and a log entry) costs little at pilot scale and avoids a confusing asymmetry.
tradeoffs: Every message now has two copies of roughly the same information in two tables. Acceptable for now; revisit if analytics.events ever grows large enough that the duplication's storage cost matters.
